demo.title: ARP MitM attack (synthetic LAN)
demo.blurb: A small office LAN. A smart plug takes over an IP via DHCP, the printer's NIC is replaced, a MacBook port-scans the NVR, then a Kali VM runs an Ettercap-style ARP poisoning attack.

alerts.message: 192.168.1.12 moved from f4:f5:d8:6e:21:12 to 24:0a:c4:9d:33:12 2s after a DHCP ACK

explanation.headline: 192.168.1.12 changed owner to 24:0a:c4:9d:33:12 (Espressif); looks legitimate
explanation.what_happened: At t = 332 s, 192.168.1.12 moved from f4:f5:d8:6e:21:12 to 24:0a:c4:9d:33:12 (Espressif). This looks like a normal change because a DHCP server handed this address to the new device 2 s earlier. Kitsune saw 15 of 460 packets above threshold around it, which is ordinary noise. ARPGuard logs it and treats the new MAC as the owner from now on.

attacker.reasoning: No attacker: the evidence fits a legitimate change (a DHCP server handed this address to the new device 2 s earlier).

impact: None expected; the old ARP cache entries on other hosts refresh within minutes

confidence.reason: a one-off binding change with normal-looking traffic

fixes.action: Confirm the change with whoever manages the device
fixes.detail: A new NIC, a replaced router or a new DHCP lease explains a one-off change; log it.
Builds the trusted IP-to-MAC table DAI checks against; mark only the uplink as trusted.
fixes.command:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
interface Gi0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust

explanation.headline: 192.168.1.30 changed owner to 00:80:77:5b:99:30 (Brother); looks legitimate
explanation.what_happened: At t = 385 s, 192.168.1.30 moved from 00:80:77:5b:10:30 to 00:80:77:5b:99:30 (Brother). This looks like a normal change because the old device went quiet before the new one appeared and the traffic pattern stayed normal. Kitsune saw 5 of 510 packets above threshold around it, which is ordinary noise. ARPGuard logs it and treats the new MAC as the owner from now on. The previous MAC was last heard 16 s before the change.

attacker.reasoning: No attacker: the evidence fits a legitimate change (the old device went quiet before the new one appeared and the traffic pattern stayed normal).

impact: None expected; the old ARP cache entries on other hosts refresh within minutes

explanation.headline: Unusual traffic with no ARP involvement
explanation.what_happened: Between t = 411 s and 427 s, Kitsune scored 1880 packets above its threshold. No ARP rule fired, so this is not ARP spoofing. The busiest anomalous flows: 192.168.1.25 > 192.168.1.11 (902 packets), 192.168.1.11 > 192.168.1.25 (898 packets), 192.168.1.11 > 151.101.1.69 (24 packets).

attacker.reasoning: The rule engine saw no ARP misuse; the anomaly model alone can't name an attacker.

impact: Unknown: depends on what the flows are (scan, exfiltration, backup, update)

confidence.reason: unusual traffic with no ARP evidence; may be benign

fixes.detail: Check whether the top talkers' traffic is expected (backups, scans by IT, updates).

caveats: Kitsune flags anything unusual: a port scan, a large backup or a new device can all look like this.

explanation.headline: 00:0c:29:7d:e1:66 is impersonating the gateway and 4 hosts: man-in-the-middle
explanation.what_happened: It began with an ARP sweep of the subnet to find live hosts. From t = 450 s, 00:0c:29:7d:e1:66 (VMware) sent forged ARP replies claiming IP addresses that belong to other devices: 192.168.1.1, 192.168.1.10, 192.168.1.11, 192.168.1.20, 192.168.1.25. It told hosts that the gateway 192.168.1.1 is at its own MAC, so their internet traffic goes to it first. The real owners kept reclaiming their addresses and the attacker kept re-poisoning them (flip-flopping bindings), which is how tools like Ettercap and arpspoof behave. Kitsune scored 10423 of 17307 packets in the incident window above its threshold, consistent with traffic being relayed.

attacker.reasoning: 00:0c:29:7d:e1:66 claimed 5 IP(s) owned by other MACs; its own address is 192.168.1.66. A VMware MAC often means a virtual machine such as a Kali VM.

impact: Passive sniffing of unencrypted traffic (DNS, HTTP, camera streams)
Session hijacking and credential theft if any login runs without TLS
Traffic tampering, or denial of service if the attacker stops forwarding

confidence.reason: rule engine and anomaly model agree

fixes.action: Turn on Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on the switch
fixes.detail: The switch drops ARP replies whose IP-to-MAC pair doesn't match the DHCP snooping table.
Builds the trusted IP-to-MAC table DAI checks against; mark only the uplink as trusted.
fixes.command:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
interface Gi0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust

fixes.action: Find and shut the attacker's switch port
fixes.detail: Look the MAC up in the switch's MAC table, disconnect it, and limit MACs per port.
fixes.command:
show mac address-table address 00:0c:29:7d:e1:66
interface <port>
 switchport port-security maximum 1
 switchport port-security violation shutdown

fixes.action: Pin the gateway's MAC on critical hosts
fixes.detail: A static ARP entry can't be overwritten by forged replies.
fixes.command: arp -s 192.168.1.1 50:c7:bf:3a:1c:01   (Windows: netsh interface ipv4 add neighbors "Ethernet" 192.168.1.1 50-c7-bf-3a-1c-01)

fixes.detail: HTTPS, SSH and a VPN keep intercepted traffic unreadable; check for certificate warnings.
